title: Commutes Sentence of Irving Stitsky
description_short: Trump commuted the sentence of Irving Stitsky as part of a clemency list.
description_medium: Trump commuted Irving Stitsky’s federal sentence on December 23, 2020. The Justice Department lists an original term of 85 years in prison, three years of supervised release and $23,152,235 in restitution for securities, wire and mail fraud convictions in the Southern District of New York. The clemency register records the grant, but not its full terms.
description_long:
On December 23, 2020, Donald Trump commuted Irving Stitsky’s federal sentence. The Justice Department lists an original judgment from the Southern District of New York: 85 years in prison, three years of supervised release and $23,152,235 in restitution. The offenses included securities fraud, wire fraud and mail fraud. The restitution award was part of the judgment alongside the prison term, so clemency should not be read as erasing the underlying financial obligation.

A commutation grants relief from punishment while leaving the conviction in place; it is different from a pardon. The public clemency register records the original sentence and the date of Trump’s action, but does not show the exact replacement terms in the warrant. It therefore does not establish how much of the prison term was removed or whether any conditions were changed. The documented event is the presidential commutation of a sentence imposed in a securities-fraud case, with the conviction and restitution amount still listed in the federal record.

title: Commutes Sentence of Jeff Cheney
description_short: Trump commuted the sentence of Jeff Cheney as part of a clemency list.
description_medium: Trump commuted Jeff Cheney’s federal sentence on January 19, 2021. Cheney had received 216 months in prison and ten years of supervised release for conspiring to manufacture and distribute methamphetamine after a prior felony drug conviction. The Justice Department’s clemency register identifies the case in Iowa and records the original judgment, but does not specify the revised sentence.
description_long:
Jeff Cheney’s federal case involved a conspiracy to manufacture and distribute at least 500 grams of methamphetamine after a prior felony drug conviction. In 2008, the Northern District of Iowa sentenced him to 216 months in prison and ten years of supervised release. Donald Trump commuted that sentence on January 19, 2021, the day before leaving office.

The Justice Department lists the original punishment and the commutation date, but its public entry does not state what sentence replaced the 216-month term. A commutation changes the punishment; it does not vacate the conviction or amount to an acquittal. The distinction matters here because the record documents relief from the sentence imposed for the drug conspiracy, while leaving the conviction itself in place. The entry also does not explain the clemency decision or specify any revised supervision requirements. Without the warrant’s terms, it is not possible to say how much prison time remained or whether other conditions changed. The established event is the commutation of Cheney’s federal sentence, not a reversal of his case.

title: Commutes Sentence of Kenneth Charles Fragoso
description_short: Trump commuted the sentence of Kenneth Charles Fragoso as part of a clemency list.
description_medium: Trump commuted Kenneth Charles Fragoso’s federal sentence on January 19, 2021. Fragoso had been sentenced to life in prison plus ten years of supervised release for conspiring to possess and distribute more than five kilograms of cocaine. The Justice Department lists the case in the Southern District of Texas and records the original punishment, but not the replacement terms.
description_long:
Kenneth Charles Fragoso was convicted in the Southern District of Texas of conspiring to possess with intent to distribute more than five kilograms of cocaine. The Justice Department records his original sentence as life imprisonment followed by ten years of supervised release. Donald Trump commuted the sentence on January 19, 2021.

The life term makes the clemency action consequential: it granted relief from a sentence that otherwise had no fixed release date. The public clemency record, however, lists the sentence that was imposed before the commutation and does not spell out the new term in its summary. It does not say whether the replacement was time served, whether supervised release remained, or whether the warrant changed other conditions. A commutation modifies punishment but does not erase the conviction. The available record therefore establishes that Fragoso received executive clemency and identifies the offense and original judgment; it does not establish the full practical terms of his release or the reason the administration selected his case.

title: Commutes Sentence of Bill K. Kapri
description_short: Trump commuted the sentence of Bill K. Kapri as part of a clemency list.
description_medium: Trump commuted Bill K. Kapri’s federal sentence on January 19, 2021. The Southern District of Florida had sentenced Kapri to 46 months in prison and three years of supervised release for two false-statement counts involving the acquisition or attempted acquisition of a firearm. The public clemency listing confirms the grant and original sentence; it does not give the warrant’s revised terms.
description_long:
Bill K. Kapri’s federal conviction involved two false statements made in connection with acquiring or attempting to acquire a firearm. The Southern District of Florida sentenced him to 46 months in prison and three years of supervised release in November 2019. On January 19, 2021, Donald Trump commuted that sentence.

The Justice Department’s clemency record preserves the original offense and punishment, making clear what the executive action changed: Kapri received relief from the sentence for the firearm-related false statements. A commutation is not the same as a pardon and does not set aside a conviction. The public listing does not state what term replaced the 46 months or whether the three years of supervision were altered. It also gives no explanation for the choice of case. Those details require the clemency warrant; they cannot be determined from the date of the grant alone. The documented event is a sentence commutation, not an exoneration or a finding that the conviction was invalid.

title: Commutes Sentence of Mary Anne Locke
description_short: Trump commuted the sentence of Mary Anne Locke as part of a clemency list.
description_medium: Trump commuted Mary Anne Locke’s federal sentence on January 19, 2021. Locke had received 234 months in prison and ten years of supervised release for methamphetamine-distribution and money-laundering conspiracies; the drug offense involved activity near a protected location. The Justice Department lists the original judgment in Iowa but does not provide the replacement terms in its public entry.
description_long:
Mary Anne Locke was sentenced in the Northern District of Iowa to 234 months in prison and ten years of supervised release. The Justice Department’s record describes convictions for conspiring to distribute at least 500 grams of methamphetamine within 1,000 feet of a protected location and conspiring to commit money laundering. Donald Trump commuted her sentence on January 19, 2021.

The case combined a drug-distribution offense tied to a protected location with a financial offense, and the original judgment included a lengthy prison term followed by supervision. The commutation granted executive relief from that punishment, but the public listing does not identify the sentence that replaced it or say whether supervision conditions changed. A commutation leaves the conviction in place; it does not reverse the court’s findings. The entry also gives no reason for the grant. Without the warrant, the record cannot establish how the clemency affected Locke’s remaining custody or the conditions that followed. What it does establish is the date of the commutation, the offenses, and the original sentence.

title: Commutes Sentence of Chalana C. McFarland
description_short: Trump commuted the sentence of Chalana C. McFarland as part of a clemency list.

The Justice Department lists a 30-year prison term, five years of supervised release and $11.4 million in restitution for a case involving bank, mail and wire fraud, identity-document and HUD fraud, money laundering and obstruction. The public record confirms the grant but not the revised terms.
description_long:
Chalana C. McFarland’s federal case involved a broad set of financial crimes, including bank, mail and wire fraud, identity-document fraud, fraud against the Department of Housing and Urban Development, money laundering and obstruction. The Northern District of Georgia imposed a 360-month prison term, five years of supervised release and $11,417,352.44 in restitution. Donald Trump commuted her sentence on January 19, 2021.

The original judgment combined a lengthy custodial term with a large restitution award. The Justice Department’s public clemency register identifies the original sentence and records the commutation, but it does not set out the replacement terms or explain whether the grant affected restitution or supervision. A commutation reduces or changes punishment; it does not itself erase the convictions. The entry therefore documents executive relief in a case with numerous fraud and obstruction counts, while leaving the specific scope of that relief to the warrant. It does not provide a basis to say that the financial judgment was forgiven or that the conviction was undone.

title: Commutes Sentence of Lerna Lea Paulson

The District of North Dakota had sentenced her to 204 months in prison and five years of supervised release for conspiring to possess with intent to distribute and distribute a controlled substance. description_long:
Lerna Lea Paulson received a 204-month prison sentence and five years of supervised release in the District of North Dakota. The Justice Department identifies the conviction as conspiracy to possess with intent to distribute and distribute a controlled substance. Donald Trump commuted her sentence on January 19, 2021.

The commutation came near the end of Trump’s term and changed the punishment attached to Paulson’s federal conviction. The Justice Department’s listing confirms the clemency action and preserves the original sentence, but it does not describe the revised term or say whether supervised release continued under the same conditions. The signed warrant would be needed to determine the precise scope of the relief. title: Commutes Sentence of Mary Marcella Roberts
description_short: Trump commuted the sentence of Mary Marcella Roberts as part of a clemency list.
description_medium: Trump commuted Mary Marcella Roberts’s federal sentence on January 19, 2021. Roberts had received 228 months in prison and ten years of supervised release for conspiring to possess with intent to distribute and distribute a controlled substance. The Justice Department’s public record identifies the North Dakota case and original punishment, but does not specify the revised sentence or supervision terms.
description_long:
Mary Marcella Roberts was sentenced in the District of North Dakota to 228 months in prison and ten years of supervised release for a controlled-substance distribution conspiracy. The Justice Department lists the judgment as entered in 2011. Donald Trump commuted her sentence on January 19, 2021.

The published clemency entry documents a change to Roberts’s punishment but does not provide the new sentence in its summary. That distinction matters: a commutation is not an acquittal and does not erase the conviction. The source records the original term and grant date, but a reader cannot tell from that listing alone how much time remained in custody, whether the supervision period changed, or what conditions applied after release. Those specifics are set by the clemency warrant. The event is therefore a presidential decision to reduce or alter a federal sentence for a drug-conspiracy conviction, with the practical scope of the relief left to the signed terms. No additional claim about the case or its outcome follows from the grant itself.

title: Commutes Sentence of Brian Wayne Simmons
description_short: Trump commuted the sentence of Brian Wayne Simmons as part of a clemency list.
description_medium: Trump commuted Brian Wayne Simmons’s federal sentence on January 19, 2021. Simmons had been sentenced in Oregon to 180 months in prison and five years of supervised release for marijuana-manufacturing and distribution offenses involving at least 100 plants or 100 kilograms. The Justice Department records the original sentence and clemency date, but its public listing does not describe the revised terms.
description_long:
Brian Wayne Simmons’s federal case involved a conspiracy and related counts concerning the manufacture, distribution or possession with intent to distribute at least 100 marijuana plants or 100 kilograms of marijuana. The District of Oregon imposed a 180-month prison sentence and five years of supervised release in 2013. Donald Trump commuted the sentence on January 19, 2021.

The Justice Department’s clemency register identifies the offenses and original punishment, then records the commutation. It does not state the replacement sentence or whether the supervised-release term changed. A commutation alters punishment without erasing a conviction, so the grant should not be described as a reversal of Simmons’s case. The published entry also does not provide a rationale for the decision. The clemency warrant would show the exact scope of relief, including any conditions that remained. The supported account is limited to the marijuana-related convictions, the original 15-year sentence and the date of the presidential commutation.

title: Commutes Sentence of Jerry Donnell Walden
description_short: Trump commuted the sentence of Jerry Donnell Walden as part of a clemency list.
description_medium: Trump commuted Jerry Donnell Walden’s federal sentence on January 19, 2021. The Southern District of New York had sentenced him to 480 months in prison and five years of supervised release for conspiring to violate federal narcotics laws. The Justice Department’s clemency register records that original judgment and the grant, but does not say what term replaced the 40-year sentence.
description_long:
Jerry Donnell Walden received a 480-month federal prison sentence and five years of supervised release in the Southern District of New York. The Justice Department identifies the conviction as conspiracy to violate federal narcotics laws. Donald Trump commuted Walden’s sentence on January 19, 2021.

Forty years in prison was the original custodial term recorded in the clemency register. The entry confirms that Trump granted sentence relief but does not state the new term, the amount of prison time remaining, or whether supervised release was affected. A commutation changes punishment while leaving the underlying conviction in place; it is not an acquittal. The public record also does not explain why the administration selected Walden’s case. Those details would have to come from the signed clemency warrant or another case record. The available facts establish the offense, original sentence and date of clemency, and support no broader conclusion about the case’s evidence or the administration’s reasons.
